generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, feedback usually points back at the same criteria your work was marked against: your grasp of the material, your clarity, and your critical use of evidence. A comment such as 'you summarise your sources rather than evaluating them' is diagnostic: it tells you where to grow next time. Running the feedback cycle turns that comment into a specific change you make in the next piece.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who get the same comment back on a piece of work: 'well researched, but you describe your sources rather than weighing them'.

Student A reads the comment, feels the sting of the 'but', and files the work away. Nothing is wrong with the reading, but it stops at a feeling. Next time, the same comment comes back, because Student A never turned it into anything to do differently.

Student B runs the cycle. Review: the comment seems fair. Interpret: it points at the critical-use criterion, and the sources really were only described. Articulate: the action is to add, after each source, a sentence judging how far it supports the point. Apply: the next piece does exactly that, and the criterion improves.

Both read the same comment. Only Student B carried it through to an action and a better next piece.
generatedProse.summary: Feedback is diagnostic: it points forward to your next piece of work. The feedback cycle gives you four stages to act on it: Review, Interpret, Articulate and Apply. The stage that carries the value, and the one most often skipped, is Articulate: turning a comment into a concrete action. You can now put the cycle in order, turn a comment into an action, and choose the move a situation needs. With learning design, marking criteria and feedback in hand, you can work with the system rather than guess at it.

check.body: A marker writes: 'your argument is hard to follow in places'. Which response is turning the comment into a concrete action, the Articulate stage?

items.text: Plan to add a signpost sentence at the start of each section in the next piece of work.
Decide the marker did not read the work carefully.
Feel disappointed and turn to the next task.
Reread the comment several times without changing anything.

feedback.correct: That's right. Planning a specific step, such as signposting each section, is the Articulate stage in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Articulate means a specific, doable step; which option names one?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Turning the comment into an action means a concrete step such as signposting each section. Dismissing it, feeling let down, or rereading do not change what you do.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
